newsitem.title: FRANCE: Gaultier launches couture with tongue in cheek.
newsitem.headline: Gaultier launches couture with tongue in cheek.

text.p: The king of French fashion's counter-culture, ready-to-wear designer Jean-Paul Gaultier, put his hand to haute couture for the first time in a show aimed as much at satire as style.

In his collection, Gaultier dressed a hulking black man in a jewel-encrusted corseted bodice while a male model with an elegantly-sculpted feminine hairdo sported a backless jumpsuit of irridescent taffeta, a floral clutch purse and nail-polish.

The women wore the simplest of garments: asymetrically- draped black crepe dresses or Gaultier's trademark bordeaux pinstriped trouser suit, fast becoming as classic an item as Yves Saint Laurent's tuxedo suit or the little black cocktail dress.

Gasultier has experimented with cross-dressing for years, but he seemed to be saying in Sunday night's show that haute couture as it is traditionally known, decked with lace, hundreds of hours worth of hand-made embroidery and wafts of precious fabric, had become obsolete and downdressing was in.
He sent out a gown of worn denim, a strapless dress unzipped down the back and, as a parody, an outlandish parrot-feather bolero.
"He is fabulously talented. He played the classic game, but with his characteristic sense of humour," said master embroiderer Francois Lesage.

Earlier, expectations that British designer Alexander McQueen might put Givenchy back on fashion's cutting edge were abruptly deflated when he sent out a theatrical, antiquity-inspired collection that resembled a costume ball.
Muscle-bound blond gods that looked down from on high, bow and arrow in hand, and a maiden strumming her harp had announced a poetic neo-classical fashion voyage.

But instead of showing off the brilliant tailoring he acquired during his years as an apprentice on Savile Row, McQueen, in his debut collection for Givenchy, put on a bizarre spectacle of large hairdos, gold-tinted breasts spilling from rib-crushing corsets and has-been snake-skin trenchcoats.

But McQueen does have talent and at times it leaped out from the gold and white mythical masquerade like an electric spark: draped chiffon birth-of-Venus dresses wound with ivy, a snowy brocade dress with billowing sleeves or an opera coat, its back painted like an Italian fresco.
Even so, it was difficult to imagine Givenchy's prim and proper clientele wearing McQueen's gladiator tunics and pheasant-feather body suits to a charity luncheon.
"It was spectacular and full of creativity. I don't think it was about wearability but he has enormous talent," said Dawn Mello, president of Bergdorf-Goodman.
"He wanted to make a statement about change. I think it's unfair to judge a designer by his first collection."
